issues.legal_issue: A summary eviction procedure cannot be used where the person in possession raises a bona fide dispute over ownership that requires adjudication by a civil court.
material_facts: The occupants traced their claim to ownership through a documented chain of conveyances and long-standing possession.
The government asserted ownership and relied on an earlier resumption notice, but that notice had been quashed by the High Court as lacking authority of law.
The history of prior proceedings and the parties’ competing claims established a bona fide, long-standing dispute over ownership.
The government had earlier told the Supreme Court that it would seek dispossession in accordance with law, including, if necessary, by filing a civil suit.
The Estate Officer issued a notice seeking eviction through the summary procedure, and the occupants challenged it by writ petition.
issues.conclusion: The Estate Officer had no jurisdiction to use the summary procedure to evict the occupants in the presence of the bona fide ownership dispute; the notice was quashed, leaving the ownership question for determination by a civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(e) and 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, the summary procedure is not suited to deciding complicated questions of title where an occupant makes a bona fide claim to possession. Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1986) 1 SCC 133, holds that a lessor seeking to enforce a disputed right of re-entry must proceed by suit, while preserving the availability of the Act where unauthorized occupation of public premises is admitted. State of Rajasthan v. Padmavati Devi, 1995 Supp (2) SCC 872, applying Government of A.P. v. Thummala Krishna Rao, (1982) 2 SCC 134, and State of U.P. v. Zia Khan, (1998) 8 SCC 483, holds that summary eviction is unavailable where a bona fide claim requires ordinary adjudication. Kaiser-I-Hind Pvt. Ltd. v. National Textile Corp. (Maharashtra North) Ltd., (2002) 8 SCC 182, and Northern India Caterers (P) Ltd. v. State of Punjab, AIR 1967 SC 1581, explain that the Act supplies a faster remedy for an existing right rather than creating a new right of eviction. The Estate Officer’s authority must be assessed consistently with these principles; Chaube Jagdish Prasad v. Ganga Prasad Chaturvedi, 1959 Supp (1) SCR 733, did not govern this issue.

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: A public authority sought to remove an occupant through a summary eviction process.
predicates.bona_fide_title_dispute: The occupant and the public authority each asserted ownership, and the occupant’s claim was supported by circumstances showing a genuine dispute requiring ordinary adjudication.

issues.definition: When a public authority seeks summary eviction and the occupant has a genuine ownership dispute requiring ordinary adjudication, summary eviction is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A lower court judgment does not merge into a superior court’s order when the superior court disposes of the appeal without deciding the merits of the issues resolved below.
material_facts: The High Court had quashed the government’s resumption notice.
The Supreme Court later disposed of the government’s appeals after the government stated that it would seek dispossession in accordance with law and, if necessary, by civil suit.
The Supreme Court did not examine the merits of the issues decided by the High Court or record findings on them.
issues.conclusion: The High Court judgment did not merge into the Supreme Court’s later order and continued to hold the field.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger applies when the superior court considers the merits of the issues decided by the subordinate court and records a finding on them. Where the superior court disposes of the matter without doing so, merger does not occur. The Court relied on Shanmugaval Nadar v. State of Tamil Nadu, (1989) 4 SCC 187.

predicates.appeal_against_lower_court_order: A party brought an appeal seeking review of an order made by a lower court.
predicates.superior_court_disposed_without_merits_r: The superior court disposed of the appeal without examining the merits of the issues decided below or recording findings on them.

issues.definition: When an appeal is disposed of without merits review by the superior court, the lower court order does not merge into the superior court’s order.

issues.legal_issue: A writ petition may be entertained to challenge the legality of a statutory notice in an appropriate case, notwithstanding an objection that the recipient should first proceed before the authority issuing it.
material_facts: The occupants filed a writ petition challenging the legality and correctness of the Estate Officer’s notice.
The High Court entertained the writ petition and dismissed it on the merits.
The Supreme Court regarded the case as appropriate for writ review because the authority to initiate summary eviction proceedings was directly challenged.
issues.conclusion: The objection that the writ petition was not maintainable was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 permits a writ petition challenging the legality of a statutory notice in an appropriate case; an alternative procedure before the issuing authority is not an absolute bar. The Court relied on Siemens Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra, (2006) 12 SCC 33, and Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, (1998) 8 SCC 1.

predicates.writ_challenges_statutory_notice: A person asks a court exercising writ jurisdiction to set aside a notice issued under statutory authority.
predicates.appropriate_case_for_writ_review: The circumstances make judicial review appropriate, including a direct challenge to the authority to initiate the action stated in the notice.

issues.definition: A challenge to a statutory notice may proceed by writ when the circumstances make the case appropriate for writ review.

issues.legal_issue: A reasoned lead opinion in a multi-judge decision states the law of the court where the other judges concur in its reasoning and conclusion and there is no dissent on the issue.
material_facts: A three-judge Supreme Court Bench in an earlier case considered whether the government could use a summary process to enforce a disputed right of re-entry.
The lead judge set out the reasoning and conclusion on that issue.
The other two judges concurred in that reasoning and conclusion, expressed views on the same lines, and did not dissent on the issue.
issues.conclusion: The reasoning in the lead opinion was the law laid down by the three-judge Bench and was binding under Article 141 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the approach to identifying the ratio of a multi-judge decision explained in The Guardians of the Poor of the West Derby Union v. The Guardians of the Poor of the Atcham Union, 24 QBD 117 (1889), and held that the relevant reasoning in Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1986) 1 SCC 133, was the decision of the Bench for purposes of Article 141 of the Constitution.

predicates.multi_judge_decision: A case was decided by a court consisting of more than one judge.
predicates.judges_concurred_in_reasoning: The judges other than the lead author agreed with the lead opinion’s reasoning and conclusion on the issue.
predicates.no_dissent_on_issue: No judge expressed disagreement with the lead opinion on the issue.

issues.definition: Where the judges in a multi-judge decision agree with the lead opinion’s reasoning and none dissents on the issue, that opinion states the binding law of the court.
